text: Why you'd branch a dbt project before a risky change, and how a branch lets you experiment without touching the working version.

Say main feeds production dashboards, and you need to rework a model's grain — a real structural change that could break downstream reports. A branch is a separate, parallel line of commits, starting from wherever you create it. Main keeps moving untouched. Little branches, big branches — they all rejoin main only when you deliberately bring them back together.

git branch, then git checkout, creates and switches in two steps. git checkout dash b does both at once. Modern Git also has git switch dash c, built specifically to make branch switching clearer. All three land in the same place: a new branch, checked out, ready for commits.

Every commit you make on your branch only extends that branch's history — main doesn't move. Switch back with git switch main, and your files on disk literally revert to main's last state. Nothing is lost — your other branch's work is safely committed, just not currently checked out.
Next lesson: merge vs. rebase — how you actually bring a branch's work back together with main.
